title: State-Machine DP: The Buy/Sell Stock Family
summary: The Buy/Sell Stock family modeled as DP over explicit holding/not-holding states — extended to cooldowns, transaction fees, and a bounded number of trades.

slides.markdown:
The Buy/Sell Stock problems teach a DP style you haven't seen yet in this group: modeling each day as being in one of a small number of **explicit states** — usually just "holding a share" or "not holding one" — and writing a recurrence for how you transition between them.

This is called **state-machine DP**, and once you see it here it shows up everywhere a problem has a small number of qualitatively different "modes" a process can be in (on/off, holding/not-holding, in-cooldown/active). The whole family — one transaction, unlimited transactions, a cooldown period, a transaction fee, at most `k` transactions — is the *same two states*, with the transition rules getting progressively richer.

slides.sectionTitle: Modeling each day as a state machine
slides.markdown:
At the end of any given day, you're in exactly one of two states: **holding** a share, or **not holding** one. Define `hold[i]` and `sold[i]` (or similarly named) as the best possible profit achievable by end of day `i`, given you end that day in each respective state.

Each day, from each state, there's a small set of allowed actions — buy, sell, or do nothing — and each action moves you to a specific next state. The recurrence for day `i`'s states is built from day `i-1`'s states plus the cost or gain of whatever action was taken. This is the general shape: **enumerate the states, enumerate the legal transitions between them, write one recurrence per state.**

Two states, `hold` and `sold` (not holding), with edges labeled by the action that crosses them: `hold -> hold` (do nothing while holding), `hold -> sold` (sell, gaining today's price), `sold -> sold` (do nothing while not holding), `sold -> hold` (buy, paying today's price).

<<< Image: two circles labelled "hold" and "sold", with a self-loop on each labelled "do nothing", an arrow from hold to sold labelled "sell: +price[i]", and an arrow from sold to hold labelled "buy: -price[i]" >>>

Every variant in this family — cooldown, fee, k-transactions — is this same two-node diagram with extra states spliced in or extra cost attached to an edge. Internalizing this picture is what makes the variants fast to derive instead of needing separate memorization.

slides.subTitle: A running-minimum scan
slides.markdown:
With at most one buy and one sell allowed, the state machine collapses to something simpler: track the minimum price seen so far, and the best profit is the max difference between a later price and that running minimum.

```python
def max_profit_one_transaction(prices):
    min_price = float('inf')
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        min_price = min(min_price, p)
        best = max(best, p - min_price)
    return best
```

This is the state machine implicitly — `min_price` is tracking the best possible "cost basis" of the `hold` state at every point, and `best` is tracking the best `sold` state's profit. Writing it this way first, before the full two-array version, helps ground the general pattern in something concrete.

slides.subTitle: Summing every profitable up-move

slides.sectionTitle: Why unlimited collapses to a greedy scan
slides.markdown:
| | One transaction | Unlimited transactions |
|---|---|---|
| State needed | Best cost basis so far, best profit so far | None — decision is purely local each day |
| Can revisit a decision | No — only one buy, one sell, ever | Yes — buying and selling is free of any "budget" constraint |
| Optimal strategy | Track running min, max the gap | Sum every positive daily delta |

The unlimited case is really a greedy problem wearing the stock-DP framing: because there's no limit on transactions and no cost per transaction, no earlier choice ever forecloses a later opportunity, so a purely local "is tomorrow higher than today" check is always safe. The moment a constraint (cooldown, fee, transaction count) makes an earlier choice matter for what's achievable later, you're back to needing the full state machine — which the rest of this topic builds out.

With a mandatory one-day cooldown after selling before you can buy again, two states are no longer enough — you need a third: `hold`, `sold_today` (just sold, in cooldown), and `rest` (not holding, free to buy).

The transition that changes: `hold[i]` can no longer come from `sold[i-1]` directly (buying the day right after a sell is now illegal) — it must come from `rest[i-1]`, the state that's had at least one full day since any sell. `sold_today[i] = hold[i-1] + price[i]` (sell today). `rest[i] = max(rest[i-1], sold_today[i-1])` (either you were already resting, or yesterday's cooldown just ended). This is the general lesson: **a new constraint on a transition usually means a new state to represent the constrained condition**, not a patch on the existing recurrence.

A flat fee per transaction (charged once, typically on the sell) subtracts from exactly one edge in the state diagram — the `hold -> sold` transition.

```python
def max_profit_with_fee(prices, fee):
    hold = -prices[0]
    sold = 0
    for p in prices[1:]:
        hold = max(hold, sold - p)
        sold = max(sold, hold + p - fee)
    return sold
```

The fee only appears once, on the sell transition, because that's the transaction actually being charged. This is a useful sanity check for any state-machine variant: identify which single real-world event the new cost or constraint attaches to, then find the one transition in the diagram that represents it — the rest of the recurrence is unchanged.

slides.subTitle: Adding a transaction-count dimension
slides.markdown:
With a cap of at most `k` buy/sell pairs, neither day alone nor day-plus-holding-state is enough state — you also need to know how many transactions you've used. The state becomes `(day, transactions used, holding or not)`.

`hold[i][t]` and `sold[i][t]` now both carry a `t` dimension, and a sell transition increments `t`: `sold[i][t] = max(sold[i-1][t], hold[i-1][t-1] + price[i])` (a sell completes transaction `t`, so it draws from `t-1`'s hold state). This is the same principle as adding the cooldown state — a new fact the answer depends on (how many transactions are left) becomes a new axis of the state, not a side variable bolted onto the existing recurrence.

slides.subTitle: day x transactions-used
slides.markdown:
Picture a grid with days along one axis and transaction count (0 to k) along the other, with each cell splitting further into a hold/sold pair. Filling proceeds day by day, and within each day, transaction counts from 0 up to k, since a sell at count `t` reads from hold at count `t-1`.

<<< Image: a grid with rows labelled day 0 through day n and columns labelled transactions used 0 through k; highlight one cell showing it split into a "hold" sub-cell and a "sold" sub-cell, with an arrow from the sold sub-cell of column t back to the hold sub-cell of column t-1 in the previous row >>>

This is O(n*k) states, each O(1) to compute — manageable as long as k isn't itself unbounded (k >= n/2 makes the cap meaningless, reducing back to the unlimited-transactions case, worth noting as an edge case).

slides.sectionTitle: Reusing the unlimited-transactions shortcut where it no longer holds
slides.markdown:
The greedy "sum every profitable up-move" trick from unlimited transactions is specific to that variant's lack of constraints. Applying it to cooldown, fee, or bounded-k versions gives a wrong (usually too-high) answer, because the greedy shortcut assumes every profitable move is free to take — which stops being true the moment a cooldown delays your next buy, a fee eats into small gains, or a transaction cap runs out.

The tell that you need the full state machine again: has a constraint been added that makes an earlier choice affect what's *achievable* later, beyond just its own immediate profit? If yes, greedy's local reasoning breaks and you need the states and transitions this topic builds — reapplying the unlimited-case shortcut out of habit is the most common mistake in this problem family.

Every variant in this family only ever reads the *previous* day's states — never two days back, and never a different day out of order. That means every version, including the k-transactions grid, collapses from an O(n) or O(n*k) array of days down to a handful of rolling variables (or a length-k array for the k-transaction case) updated in place as you scan through the prices once.

This is the same space-optimization instinct from every earlier topic in this group — look at how far back the recurrence reaches, and if it's a small constant, stop allocating a full history. For this family specifically, it turns every variant into an O(1)-or-O(k)-space, single-pass solution, which is usually the version worth writing directly rather than building a full table first, since the state count per day is already small enough to reason about directly.
